newsitem.title: USA: Christopher hails Bosnia elections as success.
newsitem.headline: Christopher hails Bosnia elections as success.

text.p: Bosnia's election was a "major victory for the democratic process" and vindicated the international community, which pressed ahead with the polls over critics' objections, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Wednesday.

Christopher told a news conference the fact that the polls were completed successfully meant the United Nations could move forward with lifting sanctions on Serbia and NATO-led troops could be withdrawn by year's end as planned.

But he acknowledged there would have to be some kind of "international presence" in the country after the IFOR (implementation force) is withdrawn, although the nature of that force has yet to be determined by NATO.
He also stressed that the obligations of Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb factions under the 1995 Dayton accords include a unified Bosnia, which many Serbs and Croats have resisted.
"This election is a major victory for the democratic process ... The large turnout demonstrated that the Bosnian people were clearly determined to go to the polls," he said.

"The balloting was orderly and calm, free of violence. This is really a remarkable achievement for a country that experienced four years of war following half a century of communism. It vindicates the international community's determination to support the Bosnia people's wish to move forward with the election on a timely basis," he added.
Although not articulated directly, the elections in fact were a vindication of the United States, which took the lead in brokering the Bosnia peace deal and insisted on holding elections this month.
Critics, including the Moslem-led Bosnian government, complained that the election was not held under "free and fair" conditions as required by the peace treaty reached at Dayton, Ohio.

But U.S. officials argued that the vote was the only way to form common institutions that could rebuild a country divided into ethnic territories. They drew confidence from U.S. Information Agency polls showing overwhelming percentages of all three Bosnian factions wanted the election to proceed as scheduled.

Christopher stressed that while the elections were a milestone, it was only one step in a long process and he promised the United States would continue to be deeply involved. He called for Bosnia to move quickly to establish the central institutions of government that the elections made possible and promised Washington would speed up reconstruction of the war-ravaged country.

Bosnia's Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic narrowly defeated his Serb nationalist rival Momcilo Krajisnik to become the first head of a new collective presidency, election organisers said on Wednesday.

The outcome was a relief to the United States and other backers of a unified Bosnia because Izetbegovic supports that goal. Christopher said he telephoned Izetbegovic to congratulate him and looked forward to meeting with him next week in New York at the U.N. General Assembly.
